 He Owes the IRS $48,000 From a 2017 Audit and Can Only Ever Send Them $200 a Month. In 2027 the Ten-Year Clock Will Run Out, and the Rest of the Debt Will Stop Existing
 Federal tax law buries a little-known expiration date inside every IRS debt, and knowing exactly how it works could mean the difference between paying for decades and watching a five-figure balance legally cease to exist.
 By David Beren 
 Published October 25, 2026, 9:48am ET · 4 min read 
 Life After Work desk. Editor: David Beren .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 Federal law caps IRS collection at 10 years from assessment, after which any unpaid balance becomes legally uncollectible.
 A partial payment installment agreement blocks IRS levies on wages and bank accounts while the 10-year clock keeps running.
 Bankruptcy, offers in compromise, and collection due process hearings can all pause the clock and push the expiration date back.

 As tax time approaches, many face the daunting task of navigating IRS forms and potential payment deadlines, like the crucial 10-year collection limit. © create jobs 51 / Shutterstock.com 
 If you owe the IRS and can only afford a small monthly payment plan, federal law sets an expiration date for your debt. The IRS generally gets 10 years from the date it assesses a tax to collect it.
 After that window closes, whatever you still owe becomes legally uncollectible. Tax professionals call this the collection statute expiration date , or CSED, and it explains how a man who owes $48,000 from a 2017 audit and can pay only $200 a month could see the unpaid balance disappear in 2027.
 Your Payment Plan Has a Built-In Expiration Date
 The IRS can approve a partial payment installment agreement (PPIA), a plan that won’t pay off the full balance before the collection deadline. You pay what your finances support each month.
 When the 10-year window closes, the IRS can’t collect the rest. An active installment agreement blocks levies on your wages and bank accounts, and the 10-year clock keeps running once a plan is active, though applying for the plan pauses it temporarily, and a PPIA might require signing a formal time extension.
 Tax attorneys say the IRS hardship pause on collection also keeps the clock running.
 Where the Ten-Year Rule Lives in the Tax Code
 The deadline is in 26 U.S.C. § 6502(a)(1) . This limits collection to “within 10 years after the assessment of the tax.” Section 6159(a) allows payment plans. Those plans “facilitate full or partial collection” of a liability. Under § 6331(k)(2)(C), the IRS can’t levy while an agreement is in effect, and § 6331(k)(3)(B) leaves that in-effect period out of the rule that pauses the clock. IRS guidance confirms the 10-year window covers the tax and any associated penalties and interest.
 Who Benefits and Who Gets Little Relief
 This works best for people who owe assessed federal tax, have limited income and assets, and hold an old assessment, like the 2017 audit in the headline. The IRS runs a required financial analysis before it approves a PPIA. Home equity, savings, or rising income could mean you’re asked to pay more, or pay in full. State tax debts follow state law, so this federal rule doesn’t cut them.
 How to Reach the Collection Deadline Legally
 Find your assessment date. Pull your IRS account transcript online. For audit debt, the clock starts when the IRS assessed the audit adjustment, which can be months after the audit ended. Each assessment has its own deadline.
 Confirm the CSED with the IRS. Ask the agency for the expiration date on each tax period you owe, and keep a written record.
 Request a PPIA. IRS Form 9465 instructions describe a PPIA as an installment agreement that won’t require you to pay the entire balance before the CSED. Expect to disclose your income, expenses, and assets in full.
 Pay by direct debit. If your adjusted gross income doesn’t exceed 250% of the poverty level, the law waives the setup fee for debit agreements under § 6159(f)(2).
 Stay current. File every return and pay new taxes on time. Missed payments can end the agreement under § 6159(b)(4).
 Moves That Quietly Pause Your Countdown
 Some actions stop the clock and push your deadline later. The clock pauses in several situations. It pauses while an installment agreement request is pending, for 30 days after a rejection or ending, and during any appeal, under § 6331(i)(5) as applied through § 6331(k). A pending offer in compromise pauses it too.
 A collection due process hearing pauses it, and the period can’t expire before the 90th day after a final determination. Bankruptcy freezes it for the length of the case plus 6 months. Living abroad for at least 6 months in a row also freezes it.
 Two other provisions can also extend the collection deadline. If you sign a written extension when you set up a plan, the IRS can collect until 90 days after the agreed date. The IRS can also sue before the deadline, and a timely court case keeps the debt collectible until the judgment is satisfied or becomes unenforceable.
 The agency reviews partial-payment plans at least once every 2 years and can change the terms if your finances improve significantly. A large balance can also lead the IRS to certify you to the State Department, which will generally deny your passport application.
 For the man in the headline, the debt ends in 2027 only if nothing paused the clock. Your transcript shows the real date. Late filings that pause the clock push the expiration date back.
